new.definition: Thin pieces of veal or beef, usually from the round, pounded flat, browned and then simmered slowly in a gravy until tender. The dish is served over grits and belongs to the New Orleans Creole breakfast and brunch table. The name is the French grillade, from griller, to grill, but grillades are not grilled: they are braised in their gravy.
new.guest: Grillades are a New Orleans Creole classic: thin slices of veal pounded tender, browned and then simmered slowly in a rich gravy, and served over grits. Despite the name they are not grilled. They began as a breakfast and brunch dish, and on our Thanksgiving menu they came to dinner over cheddar grits.
new.kitchen: The meat is pounded thin, seasoned, seared and then braised low in its gravy until a fork cuts it. The cut, the gravy and whether the meat is veal or beef are the chef’s to confirm at lineup.
new.compare: Its nearest neighbor is the breaded grillade, which the Picayune’s Creole Cook Book called grillades panées: the same pounded meat, but crumbed and fried crisp, where grillades with gravy are browned and then simmered soft. The gravy and the fork tender bite are the tell.

new.background: Grillade is French for a piece of grilled meat, from griller, to grill, yet in New Orleans the word came to mean meat braised in gravy. The printed record begins in the 1890s. The Daily Picayune ran a recipe for Grillades a la Creole on September 7, 1898, and a breakfast menu in the Times-Democrat listed grillades and grits on April 2, 1900. The Picayune’s Creole Cook Book, first published in New Orleans in 1900, gave grillades with gravy, a round steak beaten well, cut into squares and cooked with tomatoes and onion, beside a breaded version. The dish settled into the city’s breakfast and brunch tradition and into Carnival: kings and queens of the krewes keep up the custom of serving grillades and grits at the breakfasts held after their balls.

new.definition: The meat of calves, as against the beef of older cattle. Its lean is pale: the USDA’s own purchasing specification tells veal from the older calf class mainly by the color of the lean. In the United States most veal comes from young male dairy calves, and the USDA describes a typical veal calf as raised to about 16 to 18 weeks and up to 450 pounds. Cutlets and scaloppine are usually cut from the leg, most often the top round, and pounded thin before cooking.
new.guest: Veal is the meat of a young calf, paler and leaner than beef, and a meat New Orleans Creole cooks have long used for grillades. On our Thanksgiving menu it was pounded thin and simmered in gravy for the Veal Grillades.
new.kitchen: Cutlets for pounding come from the leg, usually the top round, sliced across the grain and pounded thin. Which cut the house used, and how it was braised, is the chef’s to say.
new.compare: Beef is its nearest neighbor: the same animal, older and darker in the lean. Grillades are made from either, and beef round is the common stand in, so ask the kitchen before you promise a guest veal.

new.background: Veal is treated as a delicacy in French and Italian cooking, in dishes such as escalopes and paupiettes. Veal farming spread from Europe to the United States more than a century ago, the American Veal Association says, and it rests on the dairy herd, since most veal comes from male dairy calves, which give no milk. The USDA has no codified definition of veal, and in 2020 it declined a petition from the American Veal Association that sought one based on carcass weight. In New Orleans the Picayune’s Creole Cook Book gave veal a section of its own, and its breaded grillades began with a round of veal, the cut that the city’s grillades have long shared with beef round.

new.definition: Dried corn ground coarse and cooked slowly in liquid into a thick, soft porridge, the everyday corn dish of the American South. Grits are traditionally ground from dent corn, a starchy field corn. Stone ground grits keep the germ and take far longer to cook than quick grits, which are milled finer. Some grits are ground from hominy, corn first treated with an alkali, and many are not.
new.guest: Grits are coarsely ground dried corn, cooked slowly into a soft, creamy porridge, a dish the South learned from the Native peoples who first ground corn for it. On our Thanksgiving menu they were cheddar grits under the Veal Grillades, the old New Orleans pairing of grillades and grits.
new.kitchen: Grits want a long, gentle cook and frequent stirring so they thicken without sticking: stone ground grits can take most of an hour where quick grits take minutes, and some millers advise soaking them overnight. Which grits and which cheddar the house used are the kitchen’s to confirm.
new.compare: Polenta is its nearest neighbor: both are ground dried corn cooked into porridge, but grits are traditionally ground from softer, starchier dent corn and cook up creamier, while Italian polenta is traditionally ground from hard flint corn and holds a firmer body. Hominy, the whole treated kernel, is a different thing again.

new.background: Corn porridge is Native American before it is Southern: Wikipedia traces the dish to the Muscogee, who made it from ground maize. The English word is not Native. Grits comes from the Old English grytt, coarse meal, while hominy comes from an Algonquian word for dried maize ground raw, and in colonial times the two names were used interchangeably. Grits became the daily corn dish of the South, and in 2002 Georgia named grits its official prepared food. Milling gives the dish two faces: quick and instant grits, milled finer, cook in minutes, while the older stone ground grits keep the germ and need a long, slow pot. In New Orleans grits are the bed for grillades; a breakfast menu in the Times-Democrat listed grillades and grits in 1900.

new.definition: A dish of the Basque country and Gascony, in southwest France: onions, green peppers and tomatoes softened together and seasoned with piment d’Espelette, the dried red pepper of the Basque town of Espelette. It is eaten on its own, often with eggs or ham, or used as a pepper and tomato base under other food. Its red, green and white echo the colors of the Basque flag, by coincidence.
new.guest: Piperade is a Basque dish of peppers, onion and tomato cooked down slowly together, traditionally seasoned with Espelette pepper, a red pepper of gentle heat. On our Thanksgiving menu it went beside the Veal Grillades, with the gravy, the grits and a poached egg.
new.kitchen: The onions, peppers and tomatoes are sautéed slowly until soft and their juices cook down. Whether the house piperade carried Espelette pepper is the chef’s to confirm at lineup.
new.compare: Ratatouille is its nearest neighbor: both are slow cooked vegetables of southern France, but ratatouille is Provençal and built on eggplant and zucchini, while piperade is Basque and is pepper, onion and tomato, with Espelette pepper as the tell.

new.background: Piperade takes its name from piper, the word for pepper in Gascon and in Basque, itself from the Latin for black pepper. Wikipedia gives Gascony as its home, while a French regional guide calls it a recipe of Béarn that the Basque country later took up. Its pepper came from the Americas: chili peppers reached France in the sixteenth century, and the producers of Espelette say that nobody knows exactly when it reached them, though the first traces of the pepper there appear around 1650. Piment d’Espelette is now a protected name. The producers formed a syndicate in 1993, the pepper became an AOC on 29 May 2000 and an AOP in 2002, and it may be grown in ten communes of the Basque country, two of them in full and eight in part.

new.definition: In New Orleans, the tender shreds and scraps of roast that fall away into the pan juices as the meat roasts and is carved, cooked down into a thick, meaty gravy. It is best known spooned onto a roast beef po’ boy, where it soaks the French bread. The word is the French débris, remains or scraps, and New Orleans says it the French way, DAY bree.
new.guest: Debris, said DAY bree, is a New Orleans word for the tender shreds of roast that fall into the gravy as the meat cooks and is carved, so the gravy turns thick with meat. It is what goes on a roast beef po’ boy dressed with debris. On our Thanksgiving menu it was spooned over the Veal Grillades; which roast it came from was the kitchen’s to say.
new.kitchen: Debris is what the roast gives up: the bits that fall during roasting and carving stay in the juices and are cooked down until the gravy is thick with meat. Which roast it comes from, and whether it is beef or veal, is the chef’s to confirm before a server describes it.
new.compare: Jus is its nearest neighbor: jus is the thin roasting juice served beside the meat, while debris is that juice thick with shredded meat, heavy enough to be a filling of its own. Meat in the gravy is the tell.

sources.title: Washington Times: The Messy History of the Po-Boy

new.background: Débris is French for remains or rubble, from the Middle French debriser, to break up, and English took the word in the early 1700s. New Orleans gave it a kitchen meaning and kept the French sound. The meaning grew up around the city’s roast beef po’ boy, the sandwich 64 Parishes traces to the Martin brothers’ restaurant during the 1929 streetcar strike, a story historians have since questioned. Who first named debris is disputed. Mother’s Restaurant, opened on Poydras Street in 1938, tells it as its first owner’s word for the bits of beef swimming in the gravy, served to a customer who asked for them in place of sliced roast. A 1979 newspaper account tells it instead as a play on a regular customer’s surname.

deepen.background: Poach comes from the Old French pocher, which dictionaries tie to poche, a pocket or bag: Merriam-Webster gives poché, literally bagged, and the usual account, offered as likely rather than proven, is that the set white forms a pouch around the yolk of a poached egg. The egg is where the cooking word began. In New Orleans the poached egg became a breakfast tradition of its own. Antoine’s Eggs Sardou, poached eggs on artichoke bottoms with hollandaise, is named for the French dramatist Victorien Sardou (1831 to 1908). Breakfast at Brennan’s had made its name by the mid 1950s on a menu that featured poached eggs, among them Eggs Hussarde, the restaurant’s own dish of poached eggs with Canadian bacon, marchand de vin sauce and hollandaise.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: the poached egg on the Veal Grillades
deepen.guest: Poached means cooked gently in liquid kept below a boil, so it stays tender and moist with almost no browning. A poached egg is the classic: the white sets soft around a yolk that stays runny. On our Thanksgiving Veal Grillades a poached egg sat on top, its yolk running into the gravy and the grits.
